title: Influence of wetland networks on bat activity in mixed-use landscapes
abstract: Parks and other protected lands can provide important source habitat and act as valuable dispersal corridors in urbanizing environments. However, most wetlands within protected areas are managed in isolation without consideration of the broader landscape connections. We studied the importance of wetland habitat connectivity and landscape context to bat activity in five National Parks along a gradient of increasing urbanization within the Mid-Atlantic United States. Ninety-six Anabat stations were set up throughout the parks, from which we derived the characteristic spatial scales at which bat activity was associated with wetlands. This information was used in a graph theoretic framework to construct network models of potential landscape connectivity for those species that had positive associations with wetland land cover. We found that the importance of wetlands as a predictor of bat activity varied on a species-by-species basis and increased when network measures were used that accounted for connected area in a broad spatial context. The results demonstrate that both area and connectivity of wetland foraging habitat may act as orthogonal variables to availability of roosting habitat in explaining the distribution of highly mobile species. We use the results to illustrate the value of network analysis to guide the coordinated management of two of the parks’ most valued natural resources – wetlands and bats.

## 1. Introduction

Wetlands are a valuable natural resource in need of increased protection or restoration (Zedler, 2003; Zedler and Kercher, 2005), especially in the face of current and future global change. Wetlands immobilize carbon and nutrients and are therefore important for carbon sequestration and water purification (Mitsch et al., 1995; Arrigoni et al., 2008; Knox et al., 2008); they store and slow down water and are therefore important for storm water retention and shoreline stabilization (Cohen and Brown, 2007; Hogan and Walbridge, 2007); and they produce large amounts of plant biomass and are therefore important in food web support (Bunn and Boon, 1993; Hargeby et al., 1994; Lindholm et al., 2007). Despite the recognized need to manage wetlands effectively (Zedler, 2003; Tiner, 2005; Zedler and Kercher, 2005), most wetlands are considered in isolation without consideration of the

broader landscape connections (wetland M wetland, land M - water) that many mobile species depend on to complete their life cycle (Roshier et al., 2002). Wetland management and restoration activities that do not consider the broader landscape may fall short of their target goals and waste limited funds.

Effective landscape and habitat conservation planning depends critically on the spatial arrangement and connections among habitats (Jordan et al., 2007). A single habitat patch often does not encompass the entire home range of individuals, which need to disperse to cope with fluctuating environments (Roshier et al., 2001). Graph networks have been increasingly and successfully used to describe habitat networks for conservation and restoration (Rothley and Rae, 2005; Estrada and Bodin, 2008; Lookingbill et al., 2008) and to assess connectivity among landscape elements for individual species (Bunn et al., 2000; Neel, 2008). These analyses depend critically on spatial scale (Keitt et al., 1997) where the number of nodes (i.e., patches) within a network, the area of the network, and the ‘length’ of the network (e.g., graph diameter; Fig. 1) are all strongly dependent on the distance at which a focal organism perceives landscape elements (Lima and Zollner, 1996; Pascual-Hortal and Saura, 2007). Thus, quantifying the characteristic spatial scale at which organisms are associated with landscape structure is a crucial first step in any assessment of habitat connectivity.

Fig. 1. Schematic illustrating conceptually two different measures of network connectivity used in the analysis. In the context of this study, the black patches are wetlands close enough to be connected, the gray patches are isolated wetlands. Graph diameter (Gdiam) is a distance measure defined as the shortest path connecting the two farthest apart, but connected, patches (shown by dashed lines). The area of the largest component (ALC) is an area measure defined as the collection of habitat patches with the most connected area (shown in black). As a third network metric, we also considered correlation length (CL), the average distance an individual could move among wetlands if placed randomly on the landscape.

We studied the importance of wetland habitat connectivity and landscape context to bat activity in National Parks characterized by their mixed land-use setting in the eastern United States. In addition to being a group of species of conservation concern globally (Andelman and Willig, 2002) and locally (Johnson et al., 2008), we selected bats as our model organism as they are potentially affected by both urbanization and wetland habitat availability. One limitation on bat distributions in urban settings is the availability and distribution of roost sites (Rhodes et al., 2006; Neubaum et al., 2007). The availability and distribution of wetlands and riverine environments might also be an important determinant of bat foraging activity due to the abundance of insects in these areas (Ford et al., 2006). For example, higher activity levels have been observed for the little brown myotis (Myotis lucifugus) at lakes and rivers as compared to forests and other terrestrial habitats (Broders et al., 2006), and Johnson et al. (2008) found evidence suggesting that wetland area might be a potentially important control on foraging behavior in urbanized landscapes.

We hypothesized that not just the total area of wetlands but also the spatial distribution of wetlands is critical in allowing bats to effectively use landscapes of heterogeneous land cover. We predicted that bat activity would be higher for more connected wetlands than for unconnected wetlands, as has been shown for waterbirds and other water dependent species (Roshier et al., 2001). We further predicted that the importance of a connected wetland network would differ among species, which, based on expert opinion and evidence from the literature (Francl et al., 2004; Menzel et al., 2005; Broders et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2008), appear to differ in their affinity for foraging around water, home range sizes, and roosting preferences. Because connectivity analyses are scale dependent, we assessed the characteristic spatial scale at which bat activity was positively associated with wetlands and used this value as the maximum connectance distance when constructing network models. A graph theoretic framework was chosen to construct network models of potential landscape

connectivity for the different bat species and to illustrate the value of network analysis in guiding the coordinated management of two of the National Parks’ most valued natural resources – wetlands and bats.

## 2. Methods

## 2.1. Study area

The National Capital Region (NCR) of the US National Park Service, centered on the District of Columbia and including parts of three US states (Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia), has seen rapid urbanization over the past several decades. Today the region is a highly fragmented patchwork of forest, agriculture, and developed land. The NCR National Parks, embedded within this matrix, are situated in a variety of landscape contexts from rural to urban. The parks were designed to protect both locations of historic interest as well as regionally and nationally significant aspects of natural resources, including wetland and forest resources. This array of managed parkland situated along a landuse gradient provides a useful environmental laboratory for comparing the relative effects of land-use and wetland networks on bat activity.

For this study, we selected five parks of the NCR (Fig. 2) that were similar in size, contained significant wetland habitats, and covered a gradient of decreasing urbanization of surrounding land cover (Table 1). The five selected parks were Rock Creek Park, which is forested and is surrounded by high-density, urban development; Monocacy National Battlefield Park, which is the next closest park to DC and preserves large tracts of pasture; Harper’s Ferry National Historical Park, a mix of forest and agricultural land and bisected by the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers; Antietam National Battlefield Park, which is largely agricultural (pastureland); and Catoctin Mountain Park, which is over 95% forested (Table 1). All five parks are located in the Piedmont and/or Blue Ridge physiographic provinces of the eastern US.

## 2.2. Study species

Ten bat species potentially occur within the five study parks, including big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus), silver-haired bats (Lasionycteris noctivagans), eastern red bats (Lasiurus borealis), hoary bats (L. cinereus), eastern small-footed myotis (Myotis leibii), little brown myotis (Myotis lucifugus), Indiana myotis (Myotis sodalis), northern myotis (M. septentrionalis), evening bats (Nycticeius humeralis), and tri-colored bats (Perimyotis subflavus) (Paradiso, 1969). The eastern small-footed myotis is considered rare and the Indiana myotis is a federally-listed endangered species (Best and Jennings, 1997; Clawson, 2002). All other species are relatively common throughout their respective ranges.

Eastern red bats and tri-colored bats have a stronger affinity for water and generally have moderate home ranges compared to other small bat species considered in the analysis (Menzel et al., 2005; Johnson et al., 2008). Therefore, we expected these species to be most affected by wetland networks. An affinity for water was also observed in a study done by Broders et al. (2006) on little brown myotis. Big brown bats are known to forage in wetlands in the region (Francl et al., 2004); however, their much larger home ranges should allow them to reach wetland sites that would be isolated for other species with more limited home ranges. Northern myotis tend to forage more than other species in the forest interior, perhaps at small ephemeral pools or seeps, rather than at larger, more open wetlands (Brack and Whitaker, 2001). Additional information on the roosting and foraging attributes of these species can be found in the online supplement to this article (Appendix A).

## 2.3. Bat surveys

Bat inventories were conducted as part of a regional National Park Service survey during May–August 2003–2004 (Gates and Johnson, 2005). We sampled ROCR in 2003 and all other parks in 2004. Anabat II (Titley Electronics, Ballina, Australia) broadband, frequency-division, bat detectors were used to monitor for bat activity within each park. Acoustic monitoring was conducted at multiple sites within each park between sunset and 0200 h. Each site was sampled only once for a 20-min period. No sites were revisited. Multiple sites were sampled each night, similar to bird point counts. The number of bat echolocation passes, defined as a series of echolocation pulses or calls emitted by bats as they navigate and search for food, were tallied at each site, resulting in an index of bat activity (Thomas, 1988; Broders, 2003). Echolocation passes were compared against a library of hand-released bats captured in the Mid-Atlantic region (Menzel et al., 2002). By identify-

ing the passes to species, we obtained a species-specific index of activity. This index should not be interpreted as a measure of bat abundance. Rather, it provides a relative measure of bat activity among sites.

We used the structure (e.g., frequency-modulated and quasiconstant frequency, frequency, and change in octaves per second) of recorded bat echolocation calls for species identification. We only attempted identification of echolocation passes containing P3 pulses (Johnson et al., 2002). However, echolocation passes containing P1 echolocation pulse, identified or not, counted towards total bat activity. All echolocation passes were identified by one researcher to reduce bias and increase identification precision (O’Farrell et al., 1999). Big brown bat echolocation calls were separated from all other species by a <31 kHz minimum frequency value. The quasi-constant frequency structure was diagnostic of eastern red bat and tri-colored bat calls compared to myotine bat calls, which had a frequency-modulated structure. The varying

<40 kHz minimum frequency characteristic facilitated differentiation of eastern red bat calls from tri-colored bat calls, which had a constant P40 kHz minimum frequency. Northern myotis calls were differentiated from little brown myotis calls by the slope of the call body characteristic, the former having a slope of >200 octaves per second, the latter having a slope of <100 octaves per second (Murray et al., 2001). Accuracy rates for distinguishing among myotine bat calls with the slope metric are >90% (Britzke et al., 2002).

In total, 96 Anabat detection stations were used across all five parks. These sites were located within various land covers (e.g., forests, fields, and wetlands) at each park to exploit the various foraging strategies exhibited by bat species that potentially occur in the parks and across the region (Menzel, 2003; Ford et al., 2005). The number of sampling sites located in each land cover type was in approximate proportion to that available in each park. All sites were separated by more than 30 m (minimum separation distance of 144 m; average of 2144 m), the approximate zone of reception of the Anabat II bat detector (Livengood, 2003). Five bat species were identified as present in all parks and were included in our analysis: the big brown bat, the eastern red bat, the little brown myotis, the northern myotis, and the tri-colored bat. We also combined observations for all species at the Anabat stations, including 2096 calls that were not identifiable at the species level, for an assessment of overall bat activity.

## 2.4. Landscape data

We developed land cover for the region generally following methods established by the National Park Service Inventory and Monitoring program (Gross et al., 2006; Townsend et al., 2009). Two Landsat scenes were selected that each covered all of the parks included in the study. Both images were path 15/row 33, and characterized both leaf-on (October 5, 2001) and leaf-off (November 6, 2001) conditions. We calculated Tasseled Cap Indices (greenness, wetness, and brightness) and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from the original spectral data to enhance the discrimination of land-cover features relative to image noise. To each set of spectral data and calculated indices, we applied an isodata unsupervised clustering algorithm to arrive at 100 land classes. Using high-quality color air photography (1-m resolution) attained from the National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP), we manually digitized representative areas and assigned land-cover designations to all isodata clusters. Ambiguous clusters were run through the isodata clustering algorithm a second time to achieve further discrimination before assigning a land-cover designation to each resulting class following an Anderson Level I classification scheme (Anderson and Hardy, 1976). Under this classification, the urban land-cover class includes lands of low, medium, and high intensity with a mixture of constructed materials and vegetation.

After the classification was completed, we merged the land-cover data with a raster version of the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Wetlands Inventory Data (NWI; US Fish and Wildlife Service, 2008) for inclusion as a ‘‘wetlands” category. This last step was viewed as superior to a direct classification of wetland area from the Landsat data due to the difficulty in classifying small and vernal wetlands under a forested canopy. Using an independent set of air photographs and manually digitized polygons of forest, urban, and agricultural land, we estimated our land-cover classification accuracy at 84%; the accuracy of wetland polygons matched that of the NWI (>90%; Kudray and Gale, 2000). We further refined maps with information from ground surveys where those data were available (Tessel et al., 2007).

For each of the 96 Anabat sampling locations, we calculated the fraction of land cover in urban, forest, open (grassland and culti-

vated agriculture), and wetland classes within five buffer classes: 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 m around each Anabat station. These buffers were used to estimate the characteristic threshold distance, or ‘‘foraging” range, of each bat species (see Section 2.6). We limited our analysis window to a maximum of 500 m to minimize the amount of overlap between sample points.

## 2.5. Wetland networks

Using a graph theoretic approach (Harary, 1969), we assessed the relative connectivity of wetlands for each bat species. The approach provides a visually intuitive representation of landscape connectivity and provides a computationally efficient structure for analyzing spatial patterns of large data sets (Urban and Keitt, 2001; Calabrese and Fagan, 2004). Graph networks are composed of two basic elements: a map of nodes (e.g., wetland patches) and a set of connections among nodes (Fig. 1). Thus, the model considers pairs of wetlands as either connected or unconnected using a measure of their spatial proximity. We used a Euclidean measure of wetland proximity evaluated relative to the species-specific foraging range sizes described above.

A large number of well-developed indices are available for quantifying landscape attributes based on properties of the landscape network (Bodin and Norberg, 2007; Pascual-Hortal and Saura, 2007; Minor and Urban, 2008). We chose two of these indices that emphasize different aspects of the graph: graph diameter (Gdiam) – a measure of length of the largest component in the wetland network, where a component is defined as a collection of connected nodes; and area of the largest component (ALC), a measure of the amount (in ha) of connected wetland area in the landscape (Fig. 1). Ferrari et al. (2007) provide a detailed description of the metrics. The first metric (Gdiam) is a measure of the maximum distance a bat could move from wetland to wetland within the landscape given the constraint that two wetlands must be within a given distance of each other for them to be perceived as connected. The second metric (ALC) represents the aggregate area of wetland contained in the component with the largest area and is bound by ATOT (i.e., the total amount of wetland in the landscape). In both cases, higher values imply higher connectivity.

A third graph index, correlation length (CL), has been proposed as an alternative measure of connectivity for wetlands (Roshier et al., 2001) and protected area networks (Rae et al., 2007). CL is the average distance an individual could move if placed randomly on the landscape (see Keitt et al., 1997 for a detailed description). Although calculated in units of length, the metric also accounts for patch size and all components on the landscape rather than just the single, largest component. Because this measure has been applied in similar analyses of wetland networks, we considered whether it provided information independent from the other distance (Gdiam) and area (ALC) measures.

Parks do not exist in isolation and effects of surrounding lands on nature reserves have been well documented (Hansen and DeFries, 2007a; Vina et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2009). The ecological mechanisms through which the larger, unprotected ecosystem can influence parks includes the presence or absence of movement corridors, critical source habitat, and contributions to the effective size of the protected area with implications for species diversity and abundance (Hansen and DeFries, 2007b). For our network analyses, we extended each park landscape to 10 times the maximum possible foraging threshold distance (500 m) to avoid missing important wetlands at the edges of parks. This 5 km radius circle, centered on the geographic centroid of each park, was large enough to contain each entire park except for some small outlying parcels of Rock Creek Park and Harpers Ferry National Historical Park (Fig. 2). The circles also standardized ‘landscape’ size across parks.

## 2.6. Statistical analyses

Using all 96 Anabat surveys and land cover totals within the 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 m buffers around Anabat stations, we first explored the relationship between land cover and bat activity. Following evaluation of the data to assure that they conformed to assumptions of independence and normality, we performed forward stepwise regression with the four land-cover classes (urban, forest, open, and wetland) calculated for each of the five buffer intervals as independent variables. The relative strength of wetland area as a predictor variable compared to urban and other land-cover classes was evaluated for all species combined and for each of the five focal species individually.

For bat species whose activity (detections/hour) was found to significantly vary with wetland area, the specific distance at which this positive association was strongest was used to determine the threshold distance at which that species would perceive wetlands to be connected. This perceived ‘‘foraging” threshold was assumed to be the distance a bat would travel to feed among pairs of wetlands, and is therefore the value needed to generate representative network graphs for each species. These distances may be considerably shorter than the maximum foraging distances reported in Appendix A, e.g., Bodin et al. (2006) apply movement thresholds of 5% of the maximum movement distance to account for the difficulty of crossing the inhospitable matrix in human-dominated landscapes. Landscape graphs were then generated for each 5 km radius park landscape using the threshold foraging distances.

The development of species-specific wetland networks for each park and its surrounding landscape allowed us to explore the relationship between wetland network structure and average bat activity at each park. After calculating the three metrics of wetland connectivity (Gdiam, ALC and CL), we explored the collinearity between these metrics and other landscape attributes (percent urban, percent forest, and percent open area) using Spearman rank correlation coefficients. Finally, using linear regression, we modeled mean Anabat activity across parks (in separate models for each bat species significantly associated with wetland habitat) using total park wetland area and our three measures of wetland connectivity as independent variables.

The average variation in activity among species within a park (st. dev. = 3.16) was similar to the variance in activity among parks (st. dev. = 2.86). Most of this variance was dominated by the big brown bat (Fig. 3), which had an order of magnitude higher activity in the urban Rock Creek Park landscape than in any of the other park landscapes (see Rock Creek Park in Table 1 and Fig. 2). Monitoring sites within the parks were not autocorrelated in terms of total bat activity or bat activity levels of any of the individual species.

## 3.1. Threshold foraging distances

In the regression models of bat activity within the local vicinity of the Anabat sites, wetland area was the most significant independent variable for all bats combined and for three out of five examined bat species when considered separately (Table 2). A fourth species, big brown bat, was also significantly associated with wetland area, though the strength of this relationship was not as high as for other land-cover types (negatively associated with urban land at 100 m and positively associated with urban at larger scales; Table 2). The northern myotis was positively but weakly associated with forest cover at 500 m and not associated with wetland area at the scale of this study (Table 2). Northern myotis was therefore excluded from all further analyses focused on wetland connectivity. Open cover was not significant for any species or for total bats at any of the five buffer distances.

The buffer distance over which wetland cover most significantly influenced bat activity varied by species (Fig. 4), with little brown myotis being influenced over the greatest area (500 m radius), followed by eastern red bats (200 m radius), big brown bats and tricolored bats (100 m radius). Thus, threshold distances for the network analyses were set at 500 m for the little brown myotis, 200 m for eastern red bats, 100 m for big brown bats and tri-colored bats. The threshold distance for all species combined was set at 100 m as this was the most significant distance when total bat activity was considered aggregated by all species. It is important to note that the 500 m threshold used for little brown myotis is a minimum distance, as our data do not allow us to explore relationships at larger scales. Thus, it is possible that the wetland connectivity for this species is even greater than that presented in this analysis.

## 3.2. Wetland networks

The graphs and associated metrics varied among the four species that were associated with wetlands. The Gdiam metric, the largest distance that could be traveled within the network, was especially sensitive to the choice of threshold distance. Across the three threshold distances, Gdiam was strongly affected by the presence or absence of small stepping stone wetlands and varied by an order of magnitude for four of the five parks (Table 3). In contrast, the area of the largest component, ALC, and to a lesser extent correlation length, CL, were relatively consistent for the different species within a park (Table 3).

CL and the area-based ALC metric were significantly correlated across all five parks and all three distance thresholds (Spearman’s rho = 0.70, P < 0.05). CL and ALC were both significantly correlated with the total amount of wetland area in the landscape (Spearman’s rho = 0.59 and 0.89, respectively). Gdiam was uncorrelated with any of the other measures and all three network metrics were uncorrelated with percent urban or any of the other land-cover attributes in the 5 km radius landscapes (P > 0.05).

## 4. Discussion

The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of network analysis in guiding the restoration and conservation of two valued yet threatened natural resources – wetlands and bats. The network graphs produced information for the parks that was distinct from the measures of land cover (percent wetland, percent urban, etc.). For example, Monocacy and Antietam National Battlefields are both preserved in a mixture of open field and forest land covers, and have roughly the same total amount of wetland area in the 5 km radius landscapes (3%; Table 1). However, the graph networks for the two parks were very different (Fig. 5). While the largest single wetland element was relatively isolated for the Antietam landscape, the Monocacy landscape had a number of small wetlands in close proximity to the Monocacy River resulting in a more highly connected network. Given this difference in landscape structure, it should not be surprising that Monocacy National Battlefield had higher bat activity than Antietam National Battlefield (Fig. 3).

Thus, graph networks provide information on potential movement of organisms that can supplement simple measures of land-cover percentages. That does not imply that land-cover estimates are not useful. For example, estimates of urban land cover were highly predictive of differences in activity levels for the big brown bat. We argue here that both the overall landscape context (e.g., as measured by overall land-cover percentages) and configuration (e.g., as measured by the connectivity of key land-cover classes) are important in assessing whether a landscape is suitable for highly mobile species such as bats.

## 4.1. Bat activity and landscape context

Bats require a mixed landscape that can provide both roosting and foraging sites. The literature shows a clear response of bat populations to networks of roosting sites in urban environments (Rhodes et al., 2006; Fortuna et al., 2009). We show here that total bat activity at the Anabat stations was influenced by both the

availability of wetland foraging habitats and upland habitat composition (i.e., forest, developed, open). However, activity levels of individual species tended to be predicted by either wetland metrics or upland composition, but not both (except for the big brown bat). Lloyd et al. (2006) found similar species-specific differences in the relative importance of riparian zones versus upper slopes in studying bat activity for Australian timber landscapes. Which factor is more important may depend on whether a species perceives foraging or roosting habitat to be more limiting. Foraging habitat may be particularly limiting for species with moderate home ranges but strong affinities for wetlands. In contrast, the availability of roosting habitat may be more important for bats with large home ranges that include substantial amounts of urban areas. We did not have data on the locations of roosting sites in the study area, but a direct comparison of the interaction of these terms would make a logical next step.

The importance of wetland land cover varied on a species-byspecies basis, generally in accordance with our predictions. The tri-colored bat and the eastern red bat showed the strongest affinities for wetlands. These species have small to moderate home ranges and are known to prefer to forage in the vicinity of wetland habitats where invertebrates are more common (Menzel et al., 2005; Johnson et al., 2008). The two species that had the weakest associations with wetlands, big brown bat and northern myotis, are generalist species that use multiple habitats for foraging and roosting (Johnson et al., 2008). Northern myotis was the only species associated with forest cover, consistent with their observed preference for forest interior, perhaps foraging at small ephemeral pools or seeps, rather than at larger, more open wetlands (Brack and Whitaker, 2001). Big brown bat activity was associated with wetlands (see also Francl et al., 2004), but only after accounting for their ability to roost within developed land covers. It is also possible that the scale of analysis was not sufficiently large to capture perceived differences in landscape connectivity for this highly mobile species (Appendix A).

Protected areas do not exist in isolation and the land cover surrounding a park can influence activity levels within the park in a variety of ways (Hansen and DeFries, 2007a,b; Vina et al., 2007). Our study provides additional evidence of the importance of surrounding land covers to understanding patterns of species activity within protected areas. For example, the high urban land cover surrounding Rock Creek Park may act to concentrate foraging activity within the park, resulting in the higher than average bat detections for species such as the big brown bat that can roost in houses and other urban structures within the surrounding landscape (Fig. 3). However, it is noteworthy that even for big brown bats which were positively associated with development at the 500 m and landscape levels, activity levels declined with increasing developed land cover at very local spatial scales (e.g., 100 m). A further line of evidence linking activity levels in the parks to the broader landscape context is the differences in correlation between bat activity and wetlands for different landscape extents. When the analysis was restricted to only wetlands within National Park boundaries, bat species were not associated with the availability of wetland habitat and their distribution. Only when a 5 km radius was drawn around the geographical center of the parks did significant associations between the wetland network and bat activity within parks begin to emerge.

## 4.2. Bat activity and network connectivity

Taking the local and landscape results together, we conclude that the area and connectivity of wetland foraging habitat are orthogonal variables to other land cover variables (percent urban, percent forest, and percent open) that should be considered to explain the distribution of bats in mixed-use landscapes. However,

the graph theory metrics used to characterize wetland connectivity are perhaps lacking in several regards. The area measure ALC was the best predictor of bat activity, but ALC was highly correlated with total wetland area. The Gdiam measure of network length was an independent, uncorrelated measure of wetland structure, but it had poor explanatory ability. Gdiam has the problem that it accounts only for distances between wetlands. Thus, landscapes with large, linear wetlands like Rock Creek Park may have low Gdiam values even though bats could potentially travel great distances along these linear features. We did not find CL to be any more predictive of bat activity than the other metrics.

While graph theory applications to terrestrial landscapes generally rely on patch-based data structures (nodes = habitat patches; edges = connections across non-habitat), alternative data structures may be more compatible with linear network elements. For example, Grant et al. (2007) described dendritic networks in streams in which the habitat (i.e., stream reaches) acts as the graph edges and nodes are placed at the intersections of these linear elements. This approach allows for distance along stream reaches to be incorporated in length-based measures of habitat connectivity. However, we have shown that information on patch area is important in assessing habitat quality for bats; thus representing wetlands as lines rather than patches is problematic. A more general approach is needed to analyze landscapes, such as ours, comprised of combinations of patches and linear elements. This approach would be particularly relevant to wetlands, which are often located at the intersection of the terrestrial and aquatic environments, and therefore contain structural features of both.

Another factor that we did not consider in our analysis was the heterogeneity of the matrix environment separating wetland patches. Our measure of distance was purely geographical (Euclidean distance), which assumed that patterns within the matrix had no effect on bat activity. A recent study of small mammal populations in remnant forests of human-dominated landscapes found that matrix quality was an important predictor of species abundance for roughly half the species examined, but only after accounting for Euclidean distance between patches (Umetsu et al., 2008). It is possible that variability in matrix quality could also be influencing the bats of our study, though these effects if present are also likely to be species-specific and require more detailed information on space use of bats (e.g., tracking of individual flight paths) than were available for our analysis. Our use of binary landscapes with homogeneous matrix is consistent with other applications of graph theory to avian species (Roshier et al., 2001; Bodin et al., 2006; Rhodes et al., 2006).

## 5. Management implications

Wetlands offer many valuable and irreplaceable ecosystem services to human societies including the provision of important habitat for fauna and flora. Ironically, wetlands are some of the most threatened ecosystems of the world (Sala et al., 2000) as wetlands occur where land and water meet, the same areas that are traditionally preferred for human settlement. Protection and effective management of this valuable resource is therefore paramount, and many countries have laws in place that require landowners to mitigate wetland losses. Despite these efforts, wetland landscapes continue to become increasingly fragmented leading to functional isolation of previously connected wetland habitats. We illustrated that although the conservation of total wetland area is critically important for groups of species such as bats that use wetlands as their preferred foraging locations, the preservation of connected habitat can maximize management efforts.

We argue here that well-intended and costly management efforts may fail if the foraging movement abilities of species and

the spatial distribution of wetlands relative to these movement thresholds are not carefully considered. This often requires assessment of habitat outside of distinct management units as we have demonstrated for these five National Parks in the eastern United States. At these broad scales, multiple land ownerships are common such that regional conservation efforts with multiple collaborating partners are required. For example, Catoctin and Harper’s Ferry have important partnerships with neighboring federal, state and county landowners, while Rock Creek Park has literally hundreds of adjacent landowners. The importance of regional management efforts is increasingly recognized by the US National Park Service and other management and conservation agencies (e.g., Smith, 2000; Fancy et al., 2009), but the implementation of effective habitat conservation at this scale is often held back by the lack of coherent, cross-boundary management strategies. Landscape-level analyses of wetland networks provide the type of spatial information needed to inform regional management plans.

Just like wetlands, bats are of special management concern, as many bat species provide important ecosystem services, such as pest management, and are in decline worldwide (O’Shea et al., 2003). Bats require a mixed landscape that provides both roosting and foraging sites. Roosting sites and their connectivity are known to be critical for bat survival (Carter and Feldhamer, 2005; Rhodes et al., 2006; Fortuna et al., 2009), and management efforts are often focused on preserving this important habitat component. Here we show that the spatial distribution of foraging sites may be important as well and that management of a wetland habitat network may be critical for the success of bats.

Managing bats as a group of organisms irrespective of species identity, however, is unlikely to be successful as the characteristic spatial scale at which bat species perceive wetlands differs greatly. In this study, one species was not associated with wetlands at any scale; one was associated with wetlands only after accounting for differences in developed land cover; and the remaining three species had positive associations at scales ranging from 100 m to greater than 500 m. Thus, management of bat populations relative to essential wetland resources needs to be species specific rather than targeted at the group as a whole. This is likely true for most mobile species and highlights the need for better information on life history traits such as habitat and movement preferences. Future studies should focus on integrating detailed information on individual bat flight lines, roosting locations, potential movement barriers within the matrix, and wetland configuration. Armed with this knowledge, and considered within a broad spatial context, National Parks can play a central role in conserving bat populations in urban settings by identifying, protecting, restoring, and even acquiring critical foraging habitat for these wetland-sensitive species.
